summary: Aroostook County fire tower also listed as Rocky Brook; FFLA says it still stands with its cab gone. Only a 1950 map date and statewide context found.

facts.status_note: The tower still stands, but its cab is gone (FFLA).

events.note: Maine Forestry Service 360-degree panoramic map centered on the tower is dated 1950. It shows the tower was in use by then; it is not a build date.

evidence.supports: Map is dated 1950 and places the tower in Township 11 Range 10
evidence.quote: 360 degree panoramic map centered on the Horseshoe Mt. fire tower located in Township 11 Range 10, ME, 1950.

evidence.supports: FFLA lists the site in Aroostook County, also as Rocky Brook, as standing with a missing-cab asterisk
evidence.quote: Horseshoe Mountain (Rocky Brook) Aroostook 46.58976 -68.99811 Tower Standing*

evidence.supports: FFLA legend: an asterisk marks towers whose cab is no longer in place
evidence.quote: Towers that retain their structure and support with the cab no longer in place

evidence.supports: Timberland owners began building towers after the 1903 fires; the state took them over by 1909
evidence.quote: Within two years of those fires, a group of timberland owners in Maine began building elevated observation towers on their properties, and by 1909, the state took over those privately funded lookouts

evidence.supports: Towers were staffed by lone observers who watched for smoke and flames
evidence.quote: Perched along mountainsides and ridges, Maine’s network of more than 100 fire towers was connected by telephone and staffed by lone observers who scanned the tree line for smoke and flames.

evidence.supports: Maine ended its staffed network after a 1991 budget crisis; some towers were dismantled or collapsed
evidence.quote: Maine held out for longer than most, discontinuing its network following a budget crisis in 1991.

evidence.supports: Fire towers were most numerous in Maine between 1930 and 1950
evidence.quote: by fire wardens and were most numerous in Maine between 1930 and 1950.

evidence.supports: Forest fires burned more than 200,000 acres in 1903, which led to the lookouts
evidence.quote: after forest fires burned more than 200,000 acres in 1903

evidence.supports: After the staffed system ended, some towers were dismantled or collapsed and some found a second life
evidence.quote: After the state ended its staffed fire tower system, some of the towers were dismantled or collapsed on their own and some have found a second life.

notes_for_editor: Status rests on the FFLA list and its legend (Standing* = cab gone), consistent with the brief. The 1950 date is the Maine Forestry Service map date, not a build date. No build date, height, builder, staffing, watchman or access data found; those keys are left unset. Naming caution: the Rocky Mountain tower in Aroostook (firetower.org/NHLR, US 81, ME 7) is a different site near 47.28 N, far north of this tower's 46.59 N. A Facebook group comment (seen only as a search result, not opened) says Horseshoe and Rocky Brook are synonyms; the story follows the FFLA name only.
